label: SYNTHETIC READER: a test instrument, never a reader. Fictional; not evidence about the book; not readership.

findings.quote: the designer, with the smallest scope on the team
findings.why: "Scope" is used here two lines before the page defines it (line 25), so a first reader stalls on the word with no coding background to lean on.

findings.quote: That is the point: a team of agents you cannot read is a team you cannot trust.
findings.why: It is a "That is the point" opening that follows two short sentences and states a moral the reader could reach alone.

findings.quote: The researcher could not change a slide. It could only say that a number on one did not hold.
findings.why: The narrator reports the researcher's limits with no "I" and no hindsight, as a record reader would.

findings.quote: the talk's story, the arc, the tree and the maps
findings.why: "The arc, the tree and the maps" are never explained here, so a newcomer cannot tell what the storyteller actually makes.

findings.quote: A scope is a list in a file. A check reads the list and flags any change outside it.
findings.why: A scope is already defined at line 25 and again in the quoted slide line, so the same idea is told three times in one chapter; the short sentences also run in a row (principle 7).

findings.quote: look at each of its "must not" lines and note what actually stops it
findings.why: It is an instruction on how to read, and it assumes a second agent; someone with one first app has nothing to apply it to.
A reader who opens here, or who skimmed chapter 16 on a phone, does not know who stopped what, so the chapter starts on a reference instead of its own thought.

findings.quote: the first part was never locked; nothing stopped it changing on stage but the hold.
findings.why: "Locked", "the hold" and "the gate" are never explained for someone who has only built one app, and the whole chapter's first card rests on them.
Two cards (here and line 42) are only a pointer plus a one-line quote, so they repeat chapter 16 without adding to it.

findings.quote: the slide said $17.4M a year, the 2025 edition's number, from a survey a vendor paid for
findings.why: Two figures, two editions and a vendor survey in one sentence is heavy on a phone, and the cost of the error is the point, not the numbers.

findings.quote: it was nothing sensitive, an agent that got a bit excited
findings.why: It plays down a public push of other sites' data in a chapter that says the failures stay in, and a careful reader may distrust the tone.

findings.quote: I printed a vault key into my own session log. I rotated it at once
findings.why: "Vault key" and "rotated" are used with no explanation, so the worst moment of the day lands without its stakes for a non-coder.

findings.quote: many of ruv-sgit's commits left off the "@" in front of its name
findings.why: Commit subjects and trailers mean nothing without a coding background; this is the card I would skim, and it is the least useful lesson for a next-step reader.

findings.quote: part one was never locked. I shipped the tool to lock it, then let the room's fixes crowd out
findings.why: Chapter 17 has just told this miss (lines 26 to 36) and the chapter 16 pointer at line 12 makes it a third telling; most members' "what did not" repeats chapter 17 in the same order, so a reader feels the chapter is a rerun.

findings.quote: my reviewers shared my session's reach, a second reading, not a second identity
findings.why: The phrase is abstract and arrives with no example, and "a hold any member could pull and a wake in five stages" (line 25) is as dense.

findings.quote: You met all nine at the start of the book.
findings.why: Chapter 6 says the designer arrives in chapter 8 and three more in part three, so "all nine at the start" does not match what I read.

what_holds: 06-roles-as-a-cast-you-can-read.md: "Most of their rules end with a date and a reason" and the quoted line "A scope is a setting, not a boundary" give me one idea I can carry to my own agents.

17-what-did-not-work.md: the cards that give cost, then a first-person line ("I wrote the plan down as if it were the fact") are readable and feel honest; the closing list-of-misses exercise is something I could do tomorrow.
17b-the-members-look-back.md: two answers per member keeps each entry short enough for a phone, and the security entry that refuses to invent an interview builds trust.
notes: As someone who has just finished a first app, the 'Something to try' ends are the most usable parts. The chapters assume I know commits, gates, locks and vaults; a one-line plain gloss at first use would let me take the lesson on without the vocabulary. Reading only these three sections, I could not tell where the next step for me starts.
